newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's veneer of unity covers steady decline.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's veneer of unity covers steady decline.

text.p: Zaire's squabbling political factions have united in a rare show of patriotism to denounce Rwandan-backed rebels who have seized a string of towns in its already volatile eastern refugee provinces.
Their display of solidarity has put a veneer of unity on a state whose very existence is in question.

In a country where hunger and fear are more common sensations than patriotic fervour, few believe the surge of nationalist passion is much more than a myth for the majority and a chance for politicians to compete at fervent flag-waving.
But diplomats say total collapse into civil war is far from inevitable.

"While everyone is proclaiming themselves a nationalist, in reality they see this crisis as a means of attaining their own goals and those goals are all very different," said one Zairean politician, declining to be identified.
Any kind of agreement is unusual in the vast Central African country with at least 250 ethnic groups and hundreds of political parties.

Now even opposition radicals who battled ailing and absent President Mobutu Sese Seko for decades rush to condemn the rebel mix of ethnic Tutsi and other Mobutu opponents and Rwanda, which has openly backed their guerrilla campaign.

Since October 18 Banyamulenge Tutsis and other rebels have seized a swathe of the eastern frontier and spread chaos over a much larger area. Many Zaireans felt humiliated by the poor showing of the army.
Some Zairean sceptics say the rebellion has provided politicians with a chance to compete with each other to wave the flag most fervently.

Opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, backed by thousands of student demonstrators, has used the crisis to again call for himself to head a national unity government, replacing part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.
But the position of Kengo, who has tried to implement Western-backed economic reforms, is looking more secure after a visit to Mobutu who is recuperating in France from cancer surgery.

Mobutu, who seized power in 1965, is still Zaire's most powerful figure and arguably the only symbol of national unity in a country where individual regions such as copper-rich Shaba and diamond-rich Kasai enjoy de facto autonomy.

The army, which had accused the government of not doing enough for the war effort, now says it is getting the "resources" to push back the rebels, although military analysts say an offensive may still be a long way off.
Diplomats interpreted the "resources" as back pay for the indisciplined army. Soldiers have not been paid for months and many resort to commandeering whatever they need or fancy.

The United Nations on Friday approved a military intervention force to protect Rwandan refugees in the war zone. Rwanda says it is no longer needed in light of the return home of hundreds of thousands of refugees since Friday.

"Zaire hopes an intervention force might not only give it a chance to get some influence back over the areas already occupied, but stop things where they are so instability does not spread further," said one Western diplomat.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila says he intends to take over the whole of Zaire, but so far he holds only a tiny corner of the sprawling country, which is nearly the size of western Europe.

Kabila forces have made a point of reassuring civilians they are different from the national army, many of whose soldiers, instead of fighting, turned their weapons on civilians to rob them of whatever they could before fleeing.
But so far there is little sign that Kabila has gained public support from any of the regional interests which have threatened on many occasions to tear Zaire apart.
Regions already enjoy a substantial degree of autonomy through the steady collapse of central authority and basic infrastructures after years of mismanagement and corruption.

Central diamond-rich Kasai, heartland of opposition, has used a different local currency from the rest of Zaire since Kinshasa introduced new Zaire notes in 1993 but is under no direct threat from the fighting.

Shaba, with significant copper and cobalt reserves, is closer to the fighting and has several times tried to secede before being brought back by force. So far, there is little overt sign that it is willing to fight again.
So-called Katangese gendarmes, who fought the central government for the independence of Shaba Province in the 1970s, have even asked to be rearmed so they can fight the rebels.

"National unity is as much a myth as the idea of Mobutu as an all powerful leader, but decline of the state has been gradual and it is far from inevitable that the whole of Zaire will collapse in fighting," said one Western diplomat.
